second_instance:
FOUND ON THE SWP PLANNER, 15 Aug, while wrapping that panel into rung 6. The same defect had a twin the first fix never touched, because the first fix was aimed at a page rather than at a pattern.

Four of six columns were derived beside the engine: an 'Option Drag' of balance x rate, a 'Net Hedged Balance' of balance minus that, a 'Floor Benefit' column that printed the literal words 'Floor Active' in every row under a money heading, and an 'Unhedged Balance' heading sitting over the HEDGED balance whenever hedging was on. The source comment admitted it - 'for the ledger, we show the drag on the expected path'.

Fixed the same way and at the engine this time: swpWorker records the premium charged and the shortfall the floor absorbed, per trial per year, and returns `avgPremiumPaid` and `avgFloorBenefit`. The table is Year, You Drew, Balance, Fee Paid, Floor Absorbed - five columns, all of them the engine's.

MEANS, not medians, and both by the same statistic. The floor pays in roughly a fifth of years, so its MEDIAN is zero in every row - a column of 0.00 reading as 'the floor never pays' when the truth is 'it did not pay in the middle year'. That is the sparse-series trap this codebase has now fallen into four times: the invented PAID badge, the bogus yearsFloorPaid count, the panel's sum-of-medians totals, and this. Worth stating as a rule: a statistic taken across paths says nothing about any path, and a series that is mostly zero has a useless median.

problem: Astro drops the whitespace between an inline element and the text following it when the closing tag is followed by a newline. `A bad year here means the market falls 30%.\n Serious, but not rare...` rendered as "30%.Serious", with no space. Found in rung 4, which had been through review, and in rung 5 while it was being written — so it had already shipped once unnoticed. It is invisible in the source, where the space is obviously present, and invisible in a screenshot at a glance; it shows up in the DOM as a text node that simply begins with a letter.
impact: Two sentences ran together on a reader-facing screen. Small in itself, and worth an entry because of how it hides: the source looks correct, so the defect is only findable by reading the rendered DOM. Any component that opens a paragraph with a bold lead-in — a pattern used deliberately across the rungs to name a thing before using it (dd-009) — is exposed to it.
solution:
Terminate the inline element with an explicit ` ` before the newline. The entity survives whitespace collapsing where a literal space does not.
Detectable rather than remembered: a DOM check walks every rung and flags any `b`/`strong`/`span` whose next sibling text node starts with a word character. That is what found the rung 4 instance, and it is the only reason a bug this quiet was caught at all — the pattern generalises, so checking the rendered output for a class of fault beats inspecting the source for an instance of it.

trigger: Rahul, after the rung 5 session: "the localhost at port 4321 required restart." He had to restart it by hand, which is the cost of the fault - the agent left the environment broken and the user paid for it.
problem:
Two independent faults produced overlapping symptoms, and both were rationalised away rather than acted on.

(1) STALE DEV SERVER. `preview_start` returned `reused: true` - it attached to an Astro dev server started outside this session, whose module graph had been drifting across many file edits. `preview_list` was empty, because the process was not owned by the session, so `preview_stop` had nothing to stop and there was no in-session way to restart it. The drift announced itself three times and was ignored each time:
  - a repeating `[vite] server connection lost. Polling for restart...` loop in the console;
  - two uncaught errors naming `lastResult`, a symbol that appears NOWHERE in the source tree;
  - `document.documentElement.clientWidth` reporting 0.
The second of those is conclusive on its own and was treated as a puzzle to interpret instead of proof. Verification then continued against a runtime already known to be untrustworthy.

(2) HIDDEN BROWSER PANE. Every screenshot returned a uniform navy rectangle - the root background and nothing else - at the correct scaled viewport size. This was blamed on the stale server. It was not: on a completely fresh server, with the viewport reading 1274 and the rung measuring 768x1505 at the top of the viewport with `elementFromPoint` returning a real node, the screenshot was still blank. The cause only surfaced when a `computer` action failed with 'The Browser pane is currently hidden'. A hidden pane is not composited, so captures return background only.
impact: Rahul restarted the server by hand. Beyond that: every visual claim made during the rung 5 build was made against a runtime that had visibly drifted from disk. The conclusions happened to survive re-checking on a clean server - identical values, zero console errors, same dd-008 drag result - but that was luck, not method. A screen was called verified without anyone ever having seen it.
solution:
IMMEDIATE: start a session-owned server. `preview_start` now returns `reused: false`, `preview_list` tracks the process, and `preview_stop` can restart it. All rung 5 and ledger assertions were re-run against it and reproduced exactly.

THE RULES, which are the point of this entry:
  1. A runtime error naming a symbol that does not exist in the source is PROOF the runtime is stale. It is not ambiguous and it is not worth interpreting. Restart first, then believe what the runtime says.
  2. Check `reused` on `preview_start`. When true, the process predates the session, its module graph is unverified, and nothing it serves should be trusted for verification. Restart it before relying on it.
  3. `clientWidth: 0` or a screenshot that is a single flat colour means the pane is not composited, not that the page is broken. Confirm with any `computer` action, which reports a hidden pane explicitly.
  4. When only structural verification is available, say so. DOM geometry, computed styles and text assertions are sound evidence for wrapping, overflow and sentence churn - they are NOT the same as looking at the screen, and reporting them as though they were is the dishonesty this entry exists to prevent.

GENERAL RULE: when the instrument misbehaves, fix the instrument before believing its readings. Explaining away an anomaly to keep working is how a whole session's verification quietly becomes worthless.
note: CLAUDE.md instructs `astro dev --background` with `astro dev stop/status/logs`. In this harness dev servers must go through the preview tools instead, and Bash must not be used to run them. The two instructions conflict; the preview tools are what this session used and what actually gives ownership of the process.

problem:
The swp-planner page runs TWO engines against TWO input sets and shows both to the reader at once. Found by Rahul from the screen, not by any test.

The ladder (Answer + rungs 1-5) calls swpAdviceWorker -> outlook(), at 2,000 simulations with a fixed seed of 20260815. The advanced panel calls swpWorker directly, at 10,000 simulations with no seed. Neither knows the other exists.

Reproduced at Rahul's exact inputs - 1.5 cr, 40,000/month, 30 years, 12% CAGR, 6% inflation, 15% volatility, 12.5% LTCG:
                         ladder      advanced
  survival               95.75%        95.51%
  tax paid              36.94 L       36.83 L
  balance left          17.15 cr      17.02 cr
These match his screenshots figure for figure.

The percentage-point gaps are the small half of the fault. The large half is that the ladder is STRUCTURALLY DEAF to most of the form. `readInputs()` in RetirementAnswer.astro reads three fields - corpus, monthly, years - and then HARDCODES expectedReturn 12, expectedInflation 6, annualVolatility 15, ltcgTax 12.5, annualStepUp 0. It never reads useGuardrails or bsEnabled at all. Consequences, measured:
  - Set CAGR to 10% and swings to 22% in the advanced form: the panel moves to 3.32 cr, every rung still says 17.15 cr. Wrong by a factor of five, silently.
  - Switch Buy Portfolio Insurance ON: the panel moves to 10.39 cr at 93.15% survival, every rung still shows 17.15 cr at 95.75%. So rung 5 discusses what protection costs while rungs 1-4 quietly pretend it was never bought.

The mirror that exists runs one way only - the Answer writes its three values down into the advanced form, and nothing carries a change in the advanced form back up. So the reader can put the page into a disagreeing state simply by editing the fields we invited them to edit.
impact: Fatal to the only thing the product sells. dd-003 makes correct arithmetic the price of admission rather than the achievement, and two correct-looking answers that disagree are worse than one wrong answer: the reader cannot tell which to believe and can no longer trust either. Everything the ladder was built to teach is void the moment the panel beneath it contradicts it. Rahul: "There can be no bigger failure than this."
solution:
FIXED structurally, as planned, in four parts.

1. ONE INPUT SET. `src/utils/plannerInputs.ts` is now the only DOM reader on the page. The advanced form is the source of truth; the three entry fields at the top are a two-way projection of it. RetirementAnswer's `readInputs()` - which read three fields and hardcoded expectedReturn 12, expectedInflation 6, annualVolatility 15, ltcgTax 12.5, annualStepUp 0 - is now a direct alias of `readPlannerInputs()`, so the hardcoded assumptions are gone rather than merely overridden.

2. ONE COMPUTATION. `outlook()` was split into `outlookFrom(sim, inputs)` plus a thin wrapper, which is what allows one simulation to feed many views. swpAdviceWorker now runs `runSWPMonteCarlo(inputs)` ONCE at PLANNER_SIMS=10,000 and PLANNER_SEED=20260815 and ships the raw result alongside the outlook. swp-planner.astro's own Worker is deleted; the page subscribes to `swp:result` and renders what it is given.

3. THE TOGGLES REACH THE RUNGS. bsEnabled, the hedging parameters and useGuardrails are in the shared input set, so they move the whole page.

4. A TEST. `src/tests/surfaceParity.test.ts` asserts every quantity that appears on both surfaces is identical, across a sweep of thirteen input variations including both toggles, plus guards that each assumption genuinely moves the answer - so a future regression to hardcoding would fail rather than go quiet.
detection_note: Nothing could have caught this. Every test covers one engine in isolation - swpAdvice against itself, swpWorker against itself - and the parity test that does exist, swpEngineParity, compares the two SWP engines at zero volatility rather than comparing the two SURFACES at the user's inputs. The missing assertion is not about maths, it is about the page.
second_instance:
A SECOND INSTANCE of the same fault was found while verifying the first, and it is the more instructive one. With the simulation shared, tax still printed 38.46 L on the panel and 36.8 L in the rung. Not staleness and not two runs: the panel was building its lifetime totals by SUMMING THE PER-YEAR MEDIANS while the ladder took the engine's average of per-path totals. Two different statistics wearing one label, on one screen, from one simulation.

The sum of per-year medians is also the weaker figure, for the reason that keeps recurring here: the median path in year 1 is not the median path in year 20, so the total is a quantity nobody ever lives through. It is the same trap that produced the invented 'PAID' badge in sol-023 and the bogus `yearsFloorPaid` count before that - three times in one day, in three different files. The panel now reads `outlook.flow`, so both surfaces quote one number.
verification:
Verified in the browser at Rahul's inputs, on a session-owned dev server.
  balance left   panel 16.96 Cr   rung 16.96 cr
  tax            panel 36.82 L    rung 36.8 L
  net in-hand    panel 3.37 Cr    rung 3.37 cr
Previously 17.02 against 17.15, and 38.46 L against 36.8 L.

The two silences are gone as well:
  - Switch Buy Portfolio Insurance on: panel AND rungs move together, 16.96 -> 10.26 Cr, survival 9534 -> 9268. The rungs used to ignore it entirely.
  - Set CAGR to 10%: panel AND rungs move together, 16.96 -> 7.20 Cr, and agree exactly. The rungs used to go on answering at 12%.
lesson: The fault was never in the arithmetic; every engine was individually correct and every test passed throughout. It was in the ARCHITECTURE - two surfaces each computing what they needed. dd-013: when a simple view and an expert view coexist, the simple one is a projection of the expert one. Built alongside, they diverge; built on top, they cannot. And the corollary this entry earned the hard way: sharing the SIMULATION is not enough if each surface then derives its own statistics from it. Share the derived numbers too.

trigger: Rahul, on being told sol-026 was fixed: "have you created a separate worker for the calculation in the rungs? i was expecting that i have the calculations infra done and dusted... now it seems that you have tried to reinvent fire instead of using the one already existing. the rungs were supposed to be the simple interface for the lay person or a way to decouple the complexity or simplify the complexity for the user not exist in parallel with the complexity itself."
problem:
The question was worth answering with the dependency graph rather than a reassurance, and the graph had one genuine duplicate in it.

What was NOT a duplicate: swpAdviceWorker.ts is 69 lines and contains no simulation code at all - zero matches for any RNG - and calls the pre-existing runSWPMonteCarlo. The derivations in swpAdvice.ts (outlook, findRemedies, growthCurve, sequenceRisk, protectionCurve) contain no simulation either; they SWEEP the existing engine to answer questions one run cannot - at what growth does this break, what if the bad years come first, what does a floor buy. That is a view layer, which is what the ladder was supposed to be.

What WAS a duplicate: src/utils/swpDeterministic.ts, a second independent implementation of the same withdrawal, tax and cost-basis maths. It predates this work, and its cost is on the record - the parity test guarding it says in its own comment that the LTCG double-charge 'existed in both and had to be fixed twice'. Rung 4's sequenceRisk called it, because it needed to drive the corpus along a SPECIFIED sequence of returns (same multiset, permuted order) and runSWPMonteCarlo could only draw random ones.

So the honest answer to Rahul was: no new maths, but rung 4 leaned on an existing duplicate instead of removing it. Reaching for the second engine because the first lacked one input is precisely how a parallel implementation earns its keep and never leaves.
solution:
Collapse the duplicate rather than police it. runSWPMonteCarlo now accepts `returnsByYear` - an explicit sequence of annual returns which, when supplied, drives every trial deterministically and uses no randomness. sequenceRisk calls it through a six-line `runFixedSequence` helper (one trial, zero volatility, returns supplied) and the percentile arrays collapse to that single path, which IS the deterministic walk.

swpDeterministic.ts now has no production caller. It is not deleted yet, deliberately: eleven tests use it as a harness, including the ones guarding the LTCG double-charge, and they read `growth` and `netMonthly` series the Monte Carlo engine does not expose. Those guards are worth more than the file's deletion, and porting them at the end of a long session is how a guard gets quietly weakened. Deferred with that reason rather than rushed.

The deferral is made safe by a detector instead of an intention (dd-011). src/tests/singleEngine.test.ts asserts: nothing in production imports swpDeterministic; exactly ONE `new Worker(...)` is constructed for the planner; only sipWorker and swpWorker contain the seeded-RNG markers; and no file under workers/, utils/ or Calculators/ uses Math.random.
verification:
All 39 swpAdvice tests pass unchanged with sequenceRisk on the single engine, including the sequence-risk behaviour assertions - an early downturn leaves a thinner cushion than a late one, the cushion is measured in years of that year's own spending, a failed plan reports zero. Rung 4 renders identically in the browser: cushion 20.9 years in year 1, average 10.60% a year, income never fell. The planner's shared figures still agree across both surfaces at 16.96 Cr. 153 tests green.

The first draft of the detector was too broad - it matched Math.random anywhere and flagged RelatedArticles.astro, which shuffles a list. It was narrowed to the engines' own seeded-RNG markers rather than given an exemption list, because an exemption list is how a detector rots.
lesson: A view layer earns its place by asking new QUESTIONS of one engine, never by owning a second copy of the maths. When a derivation reaches for a different engine, the honest reading is that the real engine is missing an input - so add the input. `returnsByYear` is nine lines and retired a 155-line duplicate that had already cost one bug two fixes.

trigger: Rahul asked for roughness to be explained using the last thirty years of real returns and said he had no source he trusted. I fetched secondary sources; he then supplied 434 rows of monthly Nifty 50 OHLC, Jul 1990 to Aug 2026. The primary data confirmed there was a defect AND corrected my diagnosis of it.
problem:
THE VOLATILITY DEFAULT DESCRIBES THE CALMEST DECADE IN THE RECORD AND IS USED TO PROJECT THIRTY YEARS.

swpWorker draws each year as `mu + sigma * N(0,1)`, so sigma is the standard deviation of annual calendar-year returns. The planner ships with 15 and the tooltip says 'NIFTY 50 is ~15%'.

Measured from Rahul's monthly series, 35 complete calendar years 1991-2025, price return:
  full period 1991-2025 : CAGR 13.3%,  annual-return sd 29.0%
  1991-2000             :             sd 33.6%
  2001-2010             :             sd 39.9%
  2011-2020             :             sd 17.2%
  2016-2025             :             sd  8.9%
So 15% is not wrong about the recent past - the last decade was calmer than that, and 2016-2025 contains no down year at all. It is wrong as an assumption about the next thirty years.

The decisive figure is the rolling window, because it is the only one measured over the length of the thing being projected. EVERY complete 30-year window in the data has an annual-return spread between 28.4% and 31.2%:
  1991-2020 sd 31.2% | 1992-2021 29.7% | 1993-2022 29.5% | 1994-2023 29.2% | 1995-2024 29.2% | 1996-2025 28.4%
A thirty-year retirement does not happen inside one regime. It meets several, and historically it has met about 29% - not 15%.

The implied frequency of bad years shows the same thing. At sigma 15 the engine expects a year worse than -10% roughly 1 in 14. The record has 6 in 35, about 1 in 6.
impact: Sigma feeds the single shared simulation, so this moves the survival score, rung 3's growth boundary, rung 4's sequence risk and rung 5's entire verdict. Rung 5 is the sharpest case: at the shipped 15 a floor RUINS a further 4 retirements per 100, and at the historical 29 it RESCUES on the order of 10 to 33. The screen's conclusion about whether protection is worth buying inverts on this one input - which is also the answer to the question Rahul originally asked when he settled the premium at 1.85%.
solution:
FIXED by Rahul's option 3: named periods, "which makes the assumption a deliberate choice rather than a default someone inherits."

src/utils/regimePresets.ts COMPUTES three regimes from the record at module load - never typed in, because a preset that drifted from the data it names would be a fabricated figure wearing a source:
  the last 10 years  2016-2025   growth 14.1%   roughness  8.9%   0 down years in 10
  the last 20 years  2006-2025   growth 13.2%   roughness 26.7%   3 down years in 20
  the last 30 years  1996-2025   growth 13.3%   roughness 28.4%   7 down years in 30
Each sets growth AND roughness together, because a regime is a pair - taking the calm decade's roughness with the long run's growth assumes a world that never existed. Growth is the price CAGR plus the MEASURED dividend contribution (TRI minus price over the same years, 1.43%/yr), not an assumed yield.

The default is the 30-year regime: the planner projects 30 years, and matching the assumption to the length of the projection is the only defensible pairing. The tooltip claiming 'NIFTY 50 is ~15%' is gone, replaced by the two figures and the fact that they differ.

Rung 5's roughness track carries markers at 8.9%, 26.7% and 28.4%, so the reader crosses the real periods while dragging and learns the range without reading anything - dd-008's 'mark the boundary on the control itself', applied to history.
detection_note: No unit test could have caught this, and the point generalises: the arithmetic was correct throughout and the input was simply given a value that describes a different period. The only detector for a calibration fault is checking the assumption against the world. That is an argument for keeping a sourced dataset in the repo and asserting the shipped defaults against it - a test that fails when the default drifts outside what the record supports - rather than for another test of the maths.
correction_to_first_diagnosis:
FIRST DIAGNOSIS WAS WRONG AND IS CORRECTED HERE. On the secondary data I concluded that 15% was the annualised DAILY volatility being misused as the spread of ANNUAL returns, and that the two differ by about a factor of two. The primary series says otherwise: computed over the same windows the two measures track each other closely - 1991-2000, 33.6% annual against 34.2% monthly-annualised; 2011-2020, 17.2% against 18.0%; full period, 29.0% against 25.7%. It is not a measurement error.
It is an ERA. Indian equity was far rougher in the 1990s and 2000s than in the 2010s and 2020s, and 15% is roughly right for the recent decade and roughly half of the long record. The defect is real but it is a different defect, and recording the wrong cause would have been worse than recording nothing.
verification:
Rahul's file was validated before anything was concluded from it: against an independently fetched published price-return series, 24 of 27 overlapping years agree to within 0.05 percentage points.
The three that did not agree exposed errors in the FETCHED source, not in his: it gave 1999 as +8.7% against an actual +67.4%, and 1997 as +10.6% against +20.1%. Both sat in a table that looked entirely authoritative and was cited on a finance site. That is the concrete vindication of his refusal to trust a source he had not checked, and the reason the raw file is now kept in the repo rather than a tidy derived table.
consequence: At the shipped defaults the planner reported 9,534 survivals in 10,000 and called the plan HIGHLY SECURE. On the 30-year regime the same plan reports 7,025 and the Answer now reads 'this plan is tight'. That is a 25-point swing in the headline verdict, from one assumption nobody had chosen.
correction_to_my_own_claim:
I TOLD RAHUL RAISING THE DEFAULT WOULD INVERT RUNG 5 TO A POSITIVE VERDICT ON PROTECTION. That was wrong, and the reason is the more interesting result.

It was measured with the premium still priced at the OLD 15% assumption. Once the premium is priced consistently with whatever the reader assumes, it reprices too: at 28.4% roughness the same -10% floor costs 5.73% a year, Rs 8.60 lakh on a 1.5 crore corpus - nearly twice the income being drawn. Walking the realised world across the track at that price:
  realised 10%  ->  0 ruined unprotected,  22 protected   (floor ruins 22 more)
  realised 20%  ->  8  ->  36                             (ruins 28 more)
  realised 28%  -> 30  ->  30                             (changes nothing)
  realised 32%  -> 41  ->  26                             (rescues 15)
The break-even lands exactly where the realised world equals the assumed one. You cannot buy cheap protection against a risk you have already priced in - which is the rung's own principle text made literally true by its numbers, and a better answer than the one I gave.
secondary_defect_found_and_fixed:
Repricing exposed a contradiction the screen would have shipped. The boundary sentence was computed on the analytic average payout ('nowhere does the floor pay back what it costs') while the headline columns showed it rescuing 15 per 100. Both were correct: ruin is a TAIL statistic and a floor can cut it while still losing on average. Two definitions of 'worth it' on one screen, pointing opposite ways.
The boundary is now defined on the quantity the screen actually headlines - retirements ruined - taken as the first roughness from which protection never falls behind again, so one noisy sample near the crossing cannot move it.

problem:
The premium had two sources, and they disagreed. This one is mine: P2 taught rung 5 to PRICE the floor from its depth and the assumed roughness, and left the advanced form's `hedgingDragCost` as a free input still defaulting to 1.85%.

After sol-028 raised the default assumption to 28.4% roughness the two diverged badly - rung 5 priced the same -10% floor at 5.73% while the panel and the engine still charged 1.85%. The ledger duly reported 1.76 rupees back for every rupee paid: a floor that returns 76% more than it costs, on a contract nobody would write at that price.

Caught by reading the ledger caption during verification and noticing it contradicted rung 5's verdict two screens above it, which is the only reason it was caught at all.
solution:
`readPlannerInputs()` now PRICES the premium rather than reading it - one source for every surface, by construction (dd-013). The form field becomes a readout: still visible, still carrying its figure, marked readonly and relabelled, because dd-001 asks that complexity move rather than vanish.
GENERAL RULE, and the one this session keeps re-earning: when a quantity becomes derived, every place that used to accept it as an input is now a second source of truth. Deriving it in one place is half a fix.
verification: All three surfaces now read 5.73% at the shipped defaults - the form field, rung 5's bill, and the panel's drag card - and the ledger reports 0.57 back per rupee against an engine measurement of 0.56.

problem:
sol-028's second instance, on the SIP page - and it had a worse shape than the first. On the planner, 12% growth and 15% roughness were at least INPUTS: wrong defaults, but reachable, and the fix was to give them named periods computed from the record. Here they were not inputs at all. `const eqDrift = (0.12 - 0.5 * 0.15 * 0.15) / 12` and `const eqVolMult = 0.15 / SQRT12` sat at module scope in sipWorker, with no parameter, no call site and no way for any control to reach them.

The consequence is the part worth remembering: adding the regime presets to this page WITHOUT touching the engine would have shipped a control that moved a label and nothing else. Every rung would have gone on answering at 12% and 15% while the screen said 13.3% and 28.4% - which is sol-026 exactly, rungs deaf to the assumption, arrived at from the opposite direction.

The floor depth was the same fault in miniature: -0.08 typed in here, -10% on the planner's control, and copy on both pages speaking of '-10% or -15%'. Three numbers for one contract.
solution:
Equity growth, equity roughness and the floor depth are now REQUIRED parameters of the engine. Not defaulted - required, with an error naming the missing one. A default is precisely how the last pair survived unexamined for as long as they did, and a silent fallback would let a forgetful call site go on answering at 12% in perfect silence.

The shipped page passes the named period the reader chose; the characterization tests pass 12 / 15 / -8 explicitly, so every recorded figure still describes exactly the world it was recorded in and that world is now visible rather than inherited.

GENERAL RULE: a constant that no control can reach is not a default, it is a decision - and it will outlive every intention to revisit it. When a page grows a control for a quantity, the engine must take it as a parameter in the same commit, or the control is decoration.

Debt (7.1% / 2%) and gold (8.5% / 10%) are still typed in. Same class of assumption, same problem, deliberately NOT fixed: there is no return series in the repo to derive them from and inventing one would be sol-023's fabricated figure wearing a data label. Recorded on the gate and said plainly on the page itself.
verification: Four new tests: the engine throws and names the parameter when growth, roughness or the floor is omitted; the ten-year and thirty-year regimes give different answers with the longer one both worse and wider; roughness alone drags the median down at fixed growth; a deeper floor protects less. In the browser, clicking the 10-year preset moves the shipped answer from Rs 59.4 lakh to Rs 78.4 lakh - a 32% swing that the old engine could not have produced at all.

problem:
The SIP flow rung printed a column of four figures that did not add up. Three of them - what you put in, what the market added, what you keep - described the MEDIAN path. The fourth, the tax, was the AVERAGE across all 10,000 futures, dragged upwards by the lucky ones with enormous gains. On the shipped defaults it read Rs 4.7 lakh against a real gap of Rs 3.7 lakh, so a reader adding the column up found it short by a lakh.

Each number was individually defensible, which is what made it survive being written. Found by adding the column up in the browser during verification, not by any test - the test I had written only checked that invested + growth = end, an identity that held because growth was defined as the residual and therefore could not fail.
solution:
The tax is now the tax the MEDIAN path pays: the gap between that path's before-tax and after-tax value. Because the tax is monotone in the ending balance, the median before tax and the median after tax are the same path, so the difference is exactly what that path paid and the column closes by construction. The nominal column is netted the same way, so the two columns of the rung are never in different frames.

GENERAL RULE: a statistic is only compatible with the statistics beside it. A mean and a median of the same quantity are both correct and cannot share a column. Before putting a figure next to others, ask which path it describes - if the answer differs from its neighbours, it is a different quantity wearing the same label.
verification: The reconciliation test now asserts the whole column, before tax and after: invested + growth - tax = kept, checked at both settings. It fails on the old definition. In the browser both columns tie exactly - 35.3 + 24.0 - 5.0 = 54.3 lakh in today's money, 60.0 + 130 - 16.1 = 173.9 lakh nominal.

problem: `npm run verify` ran Vitest before `astro build`. The build-output smoke test therefore inspected whatever happened to be in `dist` from an earlier build. When a new article was added, the first test run falsely reported it as unpublished even though the following build generated `/tax-code/the-loss-that-never-happened/` successfully. The check was correct; its evidence was stale.
solution: Verification now builds first and then runs the complete Vitest suite. `buildOutput.test.ts` consequently reads the artefact produced in the same command, while all unit and integration tests still run once against the current source.
verification: A fresh `npm run verify` builds the new article and passes the full test suite. The output smoke test sees the generated route rather than a prior `dist` directory.
lesson: A test of generated output must generate that output in the same verification transaction. Otherwise it is a test of workspace history, not of the change under review.

status: resolved on the SIP page; the planner is the second instance and is open
problem: Both engines assumed a fund that costs nothing to own. There was no expense ratio anywhere in sipWorker or swpWorker - not a low one, not a conservative one, simply no such parameter. Every figure either page has ever shown was computed for a fund with a zero management fee, which does not exist. This is the third instance of sol-028's shape and the worst of the three: growth and roughness were at least visible as wrong numbers, whereas this was a zero arrived at by omission, and an omitted assumption cannot be reviewed because there is nothing on the screen to review. It also happened to be the only CERTAIN cost in the whole simulation. The market may or may not fall; this is charged every year regardless.
solution: `annualExpenseRatio` is now a REQUIRED parameter of sipWorker - it throws rather than defaulting, exactly as growth, roughness and the floor do - and is charged monthly on the balance as its own statement rather than netted off the return. Netting is what made it invisible: the engine simply grew the balance more slowly and nothing on any surface said why. src/utils/fundCosts.ts supplies it as NAMED PLANS a reader could actually hold (index direct 0.20%, active direct 0.80%, active through a distributor 1.75%) rather than as a free number, which is sol-028's own fix applied a third time. The engine also reports what it charged, on the median path, in both moneys, so the flow rung shows it as a row and the column still closes exactly: put in + market added - the fund's cut - tax = kept.
verification: A guard test asserts the engine refuses to run without the fee. The characterization suite states `annualExpenseRatio: 0` explicitly, so its figures still describe the world they were recorded in rather than silently inheriting a new one. On the live page, switching the one control from a distributor plan to a direct index fund moves the shipped answer from Rs 47.4 lakh to Rs 57.8 lakh and the fee row from Rs 10.5 lakh to Rs 1.5 lakh, with both columns reconciling at each setting.
impact: On the page's shipped inputs - 25,000 a month for 20 years - the distributor's commission costs Rs 10.5 lakh in today's money out of a Rs 57.8 lakh outcome, and raises the contribution needed to reach a crore from 47,000 to 56,000 a month. The gap between the cheapest and dearest plan is roughly one fifth of everything the plan produces.
deferred: swpWorker still has no expense ratio, so the planner continues to assume a free fund. Deferred rather than rushed: it needs the same required-parameter treatment, a control, a row on the planner's money-flow rung and updates to three test bases, and doing it badly at the end of a long session is how the two pages come to disagree about a third thing. Recorded on the Launch Gate as the next item.
lesson: A missing parameter is harder to find than a wrong one. A wrong assumption is a number somebody can argue with; an absent assumption is a zero that nobody can see, and it will outlive every intention to revisit it because there is nothing to revisit. When a cost is netted against a return, the cost disappears and only the return is left to explain - which is why the premium and the payout are two statements in this engine, and why the fee is now a third.

problem: One product, one field name, two opposite meanings. swpWorker escalates the retiree's withdrawal by `(1 + inflation) * (1 + annualStepUp)`, so a step-up of zero there means HOLD PURCHASING POWER. sipWorker escalated the saver's contribution by `(1 + stepUpRate)` alone, so a step-up of zero here meant LET IT DECAY - and zero was the shipped default. The SIP page therefore modelled someone whose real saving fell by about two thirds over twenty years, while aiming at a goal the same page insisted on holding fixed in real terms. Neither engine was wrong on its own; they simply disagreed, and nothing could see it because the disagreement lived in the meaning of a name rather than in a number.
solution: sipWorker now escalates by `(1 + inflationRate) * (1 + stepUpRate)`, matching the planner exactly, in both `simulatePath` and `contributions` - one escalation constant, computed once in each, because two copies of that arithmetic is how the cost of a plan comes to disagree with the plan. `inflationRate` became a REQUIRED World parameter, since a missing rate would now silently mean a contribution flat in cash, which is the very defect being fixed. Above the engine, `contributionPlan()` in sipAdvice turns three reader-facing modes into that one parameter: `real` passes the step through, `salary` derives the rupee amount from income and share, and `fixed` computes the NEGATIVE real step that holds the cash figure still - which is the honest way to show that a flat instalment is a decision to save less every year.
verification: Seven tests in sipSequenceProtection.test.ts, including one asserting the SIP escalation now equals the planner's for the same step-up, and one asserting salary mode and real mode give bit-identical results when the rupee amounts match. Two characterization figures in sipEngine.test.ts moved and were updated deliberately with the reason recorded in the test itself.
impact: On the shipped inputs the typical outcome moves from Rs 43.7 lakh to Rs 75.3 lakh, and the contribution needed to reach a crore falls from Rs 56,500 a month to about Rs 35,500 - the page was overstating its own central answer by roughly 59%.
found_alongside: A second, smaller defect surfaced when these figures grew: `unhedgedReal` reached the hedging ledger through two roundings - to the rupee in nominal terms, then again after discounting - while the identical median reached the chart through one. They disagreed by a rupee. Rounding now happens once, where the number is shown.
lesson: Two engines can agree on every formula and still disagree on what a word means, and that is the harder failure to find because there is no wrong number to notice. When the same concept appears on two surfaces, the test to write is not 'do the numbers match' but 'does this field mean the same thing in both places' - and the cheapest way to keep it true is to make one of them read the other's definition rather than restate it.

problem: Rung 1 printed 'Rs NaN a month' where the last instalment's value should have been, and '-NaN' inside its closing paragraph. dd-017 removed `annualStepUp` from SipInputs and replaced it with a derived contribution plan; RungSipRates still read `inputs.annualStepUp`, got undefined, and rendered the arithmetic anyway. Rahul found it on the live page.
solution: The rung asks sipAdvice for the derivation - `contributionPlan()` and `instalmentInYear()` - instead of recomputing the escalation from a field it hopes is present. Its copy was rewritten at the same time, because dd-017 had also made its argument obsolete: it still said 'a fixed instalment shrinks, consider a step-up' when holding purchasing power had become the default and the shrinking case is now only true for someone who deliberately chose a flat amount.
verification: A test walks all three contribution modes plus a zero-income salary case and asserts every derived figure is finite and positive. A DOM scan of the live page for NaN/undefined/Infinity returns empty.
lesson: The compiler could not help here and that is the whole point. Rungs receive their inputs as `any` across a CustomEvent boundary, so every field access on that payload is unchecked, and a renamed field fails silently at runtime rather than loudly at build. Two defences, both used here: rungs ask the derivation layer for computed quantities instead of re-deriving them from raw fields (sol-023 at the scale of a schedule), and anything a rung prints gets a test that it is a number. A typed boundary would be better still and is not yet built.

problem: The page took its growth and roughness from REGIME_PRESETS - computed from the Nifty 50's own record - and then charged 1.75% a year, the expense ratio of an actively managed fund bought through a distributor. Rahul: 'why the fees default to 1.75%, we are using the nifty cagr and charging fees for a managed fund that may have a different cagr.' The pairing models a fund that takes the active fee and delivers the passive result: nobody sells it, nobody buys it, and it is the most pessimistic assumption available rather than the most honest one.
solution: The default is the index fund, 0.20%, because the return series being used is the index's own. The dearer plans remain and are one control away, but choosing one now states what it implicitly assumes - a manager who at least keeps pace with the index before charging - rather than leaving the reader to notice.
verification: A test asserts the default plan is `index-direct` and that the costlier options remain reachable with the caveat attached.
correction: This reverses the default chosen earlier the same day, and the earlier reasoning is worth keeping because it was wrong in an instructive way. I defaulted to the DEAREST plan on the argument that a flattering default is how sol-028's calm decade survived unexamined. That argument is about refusing the comfortable number; it is not a licence to pair two assumptions describing different worlds.
lesson: sol-028 said a regime is a pair - growth and roughness are taken together because a calm market and a generous one are not independent choices. The FEE belongs to that pair, and nothing in the code said so, which is how two separately defensible defaults combined into an indefensible model. When one assumption is derived from a named source, every assumption that describes the same instrument has to come from that source too, or be flagged as a deliberate departure.

problem: Rung 3 deducted no tax. It was not ignoring tax - it was obeying the page's BEFORE TAX / AFTER TAX button, which ships in the before-tax position, so the rung's headline outcome and its odds of reaching the goal were both quoted gross. A reader comparing the rung's figure against their goal was comparing money they would not receive.
solution: The engine now reports the after-tax median and the after-tax odds ALWAYS, alongside the gross ones, whichever view is selected - one extra pass over an array it already holds. Rung 3 shows both, adjacent, with the tax between them stated in rupees, and counts the odds on the after-tax figure because that is the money the reader can actually spend.
verification: Tests assert both frames are present and ordered at either setting of the toggle, that the gap never exceeds the headline rate applied to the whole balance, and that a gentler rate moves the net figure while leaving the gross one untouched.
lesson: dd-006 again, and it had already been applied to this exact pair of quantities one rung earlier: the flow rung shows both moneys side by side precisely because the difference is the lesson. A page-wide toggle is a mode, and a mode is the one shape a difference-that-matters may not take. The toggle survived because it predates the ladder and nobody asked what it did to each rung individually - a control inherited from an older design keeps its old semantics until someone re-derives them per surface.

problem: Rahul, on being shown the third rung-by-rung fix of the day: 'are we operating in silos, why is an update in one part of the SIP engine not updating the same thing in the other part?' He was right, and the evidence was live on the page: rung 2 printed a real rate of 6.9% while rung 4 printed 6.7% for the identical quantity. The fee had been added to rung 4's chain that morning and not to rung 2's. Separately, rung 4's growth sweep drew 300 paths per point while the Answer drew 10,000, so the same plan read Rs 90.0 lakh on one surface and Rs 89.1 lakh on the other.
diagnosis: NOT a second engine. sol-026 and dd-013 had already closed that: there is genuinely one simulation, one seed, one input set, broadcast to every surface. The silo was one level up, in the VIEW layer. The four-line derivation `real = (1 + growth) / (1 + inflation) - 1` had been written out twice - once in RungSipRates.astro and once in growthCurve - and each copy had to be maintained by hand. A new force therefore propagated rung by rung, and whichever rung was missed went quietly wrong. The same shape produced sol-035's NaN, where a rung recomputed the contribution schedule instead of asking for it.
solution: `realRateChain(inputs, growth?)` in sipAdvice is now the ONE definition of the forces acting on a rupee - market growth, the fund's fee, inflation, and what is genuinely left - and both rungs render from it. A future cost is added there once and every surface inherits it without being touched. The sweep is additionally handed the page's own full-fidelity run so its anchor point IS the Answer's figure rather than a smaller sample of the same plan.
verification: Four tests: the two rungs report the same real rate to twelve decimals; the chain reduces to the old two-rate ratio at a zero fee; raising the fee moves both surfaces by exactly the same amount, which only holds if it is one formula; and the sweep's anchor equals the full run's figures. Live check: all four surfaces now read 6.7%, Rs 89.1 lakh before tax and Rs 82.3 lakh after.
lesson: One engine is not the same as one derivation. sol-023 said a view must never re-derive what the engine already knows, and that was read as being about big things - a ledger, a simulation. It is about four-line formulas too, and those are more dangerous precisely because they look too small to share: nobody extracts a two-line ratio, everybody retypes it, and the copies drift the first time a term is added. The test that would have caught this is not 'does each rung compute correctly' but 'do two rungs showing the same quantity agree' - which is cheap to write and is now written.

problem: The insurance analyser's whole argument - the policy's yield, whether bonds or equity can replicate it, what the frictions cost, how fragile the conclusion is - was computed by one 135-line function inside a <script> tag on a 35KB page. `runReplicationAnalysis()` read the DOM for its inputs, called `new Date()` in the middle of itself, and returned pre-formatted strings like '7.22%'. Nothing in the suite touched it. Every T5 item is a change to what that function reports, so each of them would have meant editing untested arithmetic and then arguing about the result by reading it off the screen.
diagnosis: Three faults in the same shape, all of them consequences of the code having nowhere to live but the page. (a) UNTESTABLE: inputs came from `document.getElementById`, so there was no way to call it. (b) NOT DETERMINISTIC: the XIRR's calendar started at `new Date()` read inside the function, so the policy's yield was a function of the day as well as of the contract. (c) THREE COPIES OF ONE WALK: the safe route, the growth route and the sensitivity table are the same year-by-year loop at different rates, written out inline twice and again inside a nested `getEquitySurplus()`. That is sol-038's shape exactly, and on the SIP page it printed two values for one quantity. The view had begun to grow the sol-026 fault too: the frictions panel re-read `inPremium` and `inPPT` with its own fallbacks, so the premium the analysis defaulted and the premium the GST card defaulted were two decisions that merely happened to agree.
solution: `src/utils/insuranceReplication.ts` is the engine - no DOM, no formatting, no clock. `replicate(inputs, rate, taxGains)` is the walk, written ONCE, and the two headline routes and every sensitivity row call it. `startDate` is a required input. The named assumptions that were literals in the middle of the arithmetic - 7.1%, 12%, 12.5% LTCG, the Rs 1.25 L exemption, GST at 4.5/2.25%, 20% commission - are parameters or exported constants. `src/utils/insuranceInputs.ts` is the only thing that knows a form exists, on the plannerInputs/sipInputs pattern, and it owns the cover-to-premium sync as well. The page's <script> is now a view: read, analyse, render.
verification: A throwaway parity test ran the verbatim pre-extraction function against the extracted engine over six input sets - the shipped defaults, the toggle off, a policy too generous to replicate, payouts starting inside the premium term, cover costing more than the premium, and payouts ending before the premiums do - asserting the ledger, both routes, the tax drag, the XIRR string, the frictions and every sensitivity row. All matched; the refactor moved no number. It was then deleted, and 28 permanent tests took its place in `insuranceReplication.test.ts`, including the one that says the sensitivity table's baseline row must EQUAL the headline growth figure - the assertion that makes the third copy of the walk impossible to reintroduce.
lesson: The extraction is not preparation for the work; it IS the work. Three of the four remaining T5 items are claims about the sign and the wording of figures this function produces, and none of them could be argued about until the figures could be asserted. Within an hour of the engine being callable it had already reported, in a test rather than in an argument: the safe route ends Rs 11.08 lakh SHORT at the shipped defaults while the page prints that number in emerald green under the word 'Surplus'; the bottom line calls a negative number 'SURPLUS WEALTH'; the safe route is charged no tax at all, which flatters the very route the page uses to argue the policy is beatable risk-free; the LTCG exemption is applied once to a terminal gain rather than annually; the maturity field turns a typed 0 back into Rs 10 lakh, against its own tooltip; and the walk lets an exhausted portfolio go negative and keeps compounding it, so the sensitivity table can tell a reader that a HIGHER return leaves them worse off - the deficit is worst around 11%, not at 8%. None of that was found by reading the page. All of it was found by being able to call the function.
